entry.title: Farewell Views of the Skyscrapers
entry.summary: For the last time this year, the alarms on our telephones rang out on Korean soil, announcing that it was time to rise. With our luggage ready, we headed to the earliest possible breakfast sitting and, with sleepy eyes, took one last look at the skyscrapers and parks from the Oakwood Premier hotel.
entry.content:
For the last time this year, the alarms on our telephones rang out on Korean soil, announcing that it was time to rise. With our luggage ready, we headed to the earliest possible breakfast sitting and, with sleepy eyes, took one last look at the skyscrapers and parks from the Oakwood Premier hotel.

Before we could even say thank you in Korean, we had already handed our key cards to the lady at reception and descended 36 floors to await our coach to Incheon Airport. A calm ride, a city waking up, the Incheon sign on a hill in the distance and a view of the airport say it all. At the airport, we used the last pieces of cling film to wrap our suitcases, drank the last drops of our drinks and joined the check-in queue to the sound of the machines that push luggage trolleys and play Beethoven’s Für Elise as they go. Before dropping off our bags, we had to take a few things out of our rucksacks, as this time we were warned that a rucksack and a small suitcase together may not weigh more than 10 kg. Once everything was out and weighed, we could pack it all back in. We waited another ten minutes in case we were called back over anything unsuitable in our checked-in luggage (such as a robot).

Soon we made our way through security, past the shops and the tax refund stations for foreign shoppers, all the way to our boarding gate. We then allowed ourselves some rest and strolled about the shops, past a re-enactment of a royal procession and purveyors of doughnuts, souvenirs and magnets. We bade farewell to Jaka, the Slovenian FIRST volunteer, and boarded an aeroplane that was less spacious and luxurious than the one that had carried us to Korea. Dripping air conditioning and heat transfer are not the most commendable features of an aeroplane with Rolls-Royce written on it.

So, with films, sleep, dinner and breakfast, we once again crossed numerous time zones and soon began our five-hour stopover in Warsaw, with automated border control followed by a hunt for a seat, a nap or a stroll in search of food. We slept through the flight to Zagreb, and at the airport we collected our suitcases, counted our hats and set off for our ride home in an extended fire brigade van.

Until next time

hayrli tun

entry.title: So, Where to Next Year?
entry.summary: At breakfast, we wished each other ‘Gud monin’, as our friends from the Solomon Islands would say, and chatted whilst clearing our plates. Then we quickened our pace to get ready as soon as possible for the last three matches of our firefighting attempt at this year’s robotics Olympics, the FIRST Global Challenge.
entry.content:
At breakfast, we wished each other ‘Gud monin’, as our friends from the Solomon Islands would say, and chatted whilst clearing our plates. Then we quickened our pace to get ready as soon as possible for the last three matches of our firefighting attempt at this year’s robotics Olympics, the FIRST Global Challenge.

Before the first match, our peers from Uruguay and the Gambia called by so that we could agree on how to work together, as a co-operative showdown awaited us against the red alliance, namely Greece, Papua New Guinea and the host country, South Korea. The queue was pleasant, the match short and the result good, but not good enough. We scored 129 points, whilst our opponents scored 278, and thus match 253 came to an end.

Today was the last day of the event, so we encouraged the students to start looking for shirt swap candidates. Whilst searching, they offered tastings of Herba sweets and Cockta, which delighted the volunteers, the other competitors and absolutely everyone else. We managed to arrange swaps with our friends from Slovakia and South Africa, and some even organised a swap with the team from Chile across the bushes.

A couple of sweets later, we were called back to the queue, this time for match number 279. The competition was somewhat more modest on both sides: we represented the red side together with Lesotho and Iran, whilst the blue side was represented by Palestine, Eritrea and Cape Verde. Fighting the fire took two minutes and thirty seconds and ended 71 : 50 in our favour. To recharge, we treated ourselves to one last lunch break with snacks.

All the hard work brought us to our last match before the end of the qualification rounds. We confidently shook hands with our old friends from Venezuela and left the students to agree with the team from Luxembourg on how to play the final match. They stepped up to the stage, with their peers from Myanmar, Yemen and Haiti on the other side. Clear communication, plenty of balls and climbing robots were unfortunately not enough. We applauded everyone, despite the 240 : 178 result to our opponents.

Whilst waiting for the announcement of the top 24 countries and the eight randomly drawn wildcard countries, each of us passed the time chatting with someone from some corner of the world, which is precisely the charm of this competition. Unfortunately, we were not picked, so we could pack up early and take our things back to the hotel. Upon our return, we cheered on our friends from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who had made it into the top 24. Montenegro was drawn as a wildcard, but they had already packed away everything they could before the announcement, so Kazakhstan’s urgent strategy session caught them entirely off guard.

We spent the remaining minutes with friends who would be leaving Korea before midnight, and in the stands, cheering at the top of our lungs for the Slovak team in the New Technology Experience side competition. Their idea of detecting fires by sound was an interesting one and earned them third place on the podium, and with it Slovakia’s first medal. We also warmed up our hands applauding the announcement of the best mentors, with the mentors of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of Slovakia amongst the nominees.

We handed out the last few keyrings and drops of Cockta to those who had made the Slovenian pit their safe space. Then we made our way to the stands for the closing ceremony. We were treated to the final matches, karate-style K-pop performances and the announcement of the 2027 venue. And next year we shall be breaking wheels, blowing fuses and sharing smiles with friends from all over the world nowhere else but in Madrid, Spain.

We grabbed the last snacks and bade farewell to all the wonderful volunteers, organisers and participants. Then we set off towards the Hyundai Outlet Centre, some by Uber and others along the running track. What awaited us at the end of the kilometre-long park was a shopping centre that sorts its shops by floor: children’s, men’s, women’s, and general in the basement. And along the open-air walkways, sculptures, yachts, stalls and cafés.

The general section was the most interesting to us, as the basement hid everything from a Nintendo shop, IKEA and a bookshop with a pile of mechanical keyboards to premium clothing and footwear shops that liked to greet customers with stands for their drinks. Curious shoppers also discovered a tempting corridor that revealed ever more restaurants the further one walked. And if one headed to the upper levels of the corridor, one found oneself in another shopping centre called Triple Street, where the buildings are labelled A to D, with small parks and places to rest in between. So we strolled past cafés and restaurants serving Korean barbecue or fast food, and at the end of the walkway, we came out onto the main road.

The late hour beckoned us back home through YingYang Park, where besides large open spaces we also found a soothing barefoot walking path, which one finishes by cleaning the soles of one’s feet with an air blower.

It would not do to come home without spices, so before bed we popped into the by now familiar Lotte Mart, bought souvenirs, sauces and snacks, and retired to our hotel rooms. We had a visit from Trym, a Norwegian student who came to swap shirts with our students and stayed longer than expected. Before getting some rest, there was still the packing and weighing of suitcases to be done, and the shifting of luggage into the spaces where we had previously packed 12 litres of Cockta.

Until next time

goeie nag

entry.title: Wins, Cockta and a Festive Chinatown
entry.summary: We began the ninth of October in the same manner as every day so far, but with a heartier breakfast, since no fewer than five matches awaited us. Motivated and well fed, we headed to the pit with our hats upon our heads.
entry.content:
We began the ninth of October in the same manner as every day so far, but with a heartier breakfast, since no fewer than five matches awaited us. Motivated and well fed, we headed to the pit with our hats upon our heads.

Our students were soon visited by their new alliance partners, and they agreed that our main role would be to collect balls and pass them into the container of the human player, who would then throw them into the basket by hand. With some time to spare, the students dashed off in their straw hats for a photograph, whilst the Slovak mentors chatted with us about Holy Priest performing in Bratislava in November, which sparked a debate about electronic music.

It was time for match number 93, in which we once again represented the blue alliance, together with the teams from Australia and Jordan. A modest strategy combined with climbing robots served us well, as we managed to finish the match ‘against’ Belarus, Azerbaijan and the Comoros 56 : 39 in our favour.

Soon the countries that sit close together in the alphabet had to gather once again. In match number 132, the red alliance was made up of Slovenia, Somalia and Sierra Leone. With every press of a gamepad button, the timer showed a lower number, and when it reached the end, we shook hands with our friends on the other side from Tanzania, Mozambique and Montenegro and congratulated them on a well-deserved win.

During the break, we visited the stands of Korean and American universities and of this year’s sponsor LG, who had brought along a Lego model and a mobile robot. A few photographs and a few words later, we were already walking back to the pit. Soon a volunteer came to fetch us and invited us into the queue together with Turkmenistan and Mongolia, who were also on the blue alliance. Across the table, we greeted the teams from Thailand, the British Virgin Islands and Eswatini. Match number 162 soon began, and after 150 seconds we all applauded, even though the final score was 195 : 81 to the blue side.

The students ran happily back to the pit, set the robot down, gave the M3 screws and nuts a few turns with the Allen key and went off for a lunch break and snacks with other countries. The break was followed by a discussion with our friends from the Solomon Islands and Denmark, so that they could clarify what each robot can do and forge a winning strategy. As every time so far, a volunteer tugged at our team’s sleeves to send them to the queue and on to the field for match number 201. The announcer introduced our blue side and, of course, the red side, where we could see the flags of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tunisia and Zimbabwe. We successfully put out the fire in the form of orange balls, with our side scoring 171 points and finishing the match on a high.

For the last match of the day, we put our heads together with our friends from Guinea and Senegal. Although our chances of winning were slim, we nevertheless threw ourselves into a co-operative game against Finland, Micronesia and American Samoa. We did not end the day on a high note, as we shook hands after a 189 : 36 result to the opposing alliance.

Sharing our impressions of the day over dinner by the famous guest chef Irvine was a pleasant experience, with American cuisine on the menu. We ate quickly, dropped our things off at the hotel and caught the number 16 bus to the city’s Chinatown.

On the way, we rode past the war memorial we had visited the other day, and alighted at the Sinpo Market stop. We took a quick look at the outside of a church just a few steps from the main road. From up there, we had a fine view of the entrance to the open-air Chinese food market, where we found fruit for sale and fresh dumplings, as everything else had sadly already closed. At the end of the market, the illuminated streets of the Chinatown district opened up before us. We were looking for a festival, so we followed the biggest crowds. After walking past countless cafés and Korean barbecue restaurants, we arrived at a sign reading ‘Incheon Open Port Culture Night’.

From here on, we were part of the festival, with stalls full of trinkets, goulash and Pokémon cards. A stroll past complete strangers led us to singing performances, solo performances on wind instruments and violins and, on the big stage, singing to a saxophone accompaniment of ‘It’s Raining Men’. The applause from every direction encouraged us to explore the other streets as well, where we met the ladies from our robotics event’s tourist stand, who gave us some local sweets and train tickets and captured the moment in a photograph. After that, we rolled the moon for a picture and headed for the exit of the culture night. Before leaving, we bought a couple of fans and some Chinese coins and continued on towards the fairy tale village.

On the way to the ‘FairyTale Village’, we came across a small shop selling snacks and drinks, where we were pleasantly surprised to find the first fridge magnets in the city, which we simply had to have. Refreshed, we continued through the village, where we found letters in a vending machine and sculptures of the Wizard of Oz, Pinocchio and other cartoon characters. At the end of the street, we found steps that led us up to an illuminated woodland path with animal sculptures. At the top of the climb, we found a sky observatory, from where we swiftly continued down the hill, past raccoons and a park with water projections. Hoping to catch the last bus, we studied the timetables at the stops, but once again we had to admit defeat and call an Uber.

Until next time,

gutnaet

entry.title: New Results, New Faces at the Party
entry.summary: A new date, new treats on the breakfast menu. We quickly warmed up our shoes with an early walk from the hotel to the arena, where over the next few days the robots will prove their worth, and with them the young people upon whom the world rests.
entry.content:
A new date, new treats on the breakfast menu. We quickly warmed up our shoes with an early walk from the hotel to the arena, where over the next few days the robots will prove their worth, and with them the young people upon whom the world rests.

During the final repairs to the robot, we received a sheet of paper with the match schedule, which also showed us our alliance partners and our opponents. Some countries had prepared for this in advance by sending team members to visit the pits of every other country, where they filled in a questionnaire on their own platform whilst looking at each robot, gathering information about what every country’s robot can do. The most competitive countries went through this process twice, going to help the weaker countries on their alliance, whilst some countries gathered all six countries of a given match to agree on how to score as many points as possible together, since that is the only way everyone can achieve the highest possible score.

Forging strategies, along with the last repairs to the robot, brought us to the practice match, which gave the drive team a touch of stage fright.

We played match number 19 on the red side together with Burkina Faso and Cuba, whilst the blue side was graced by Paraguay, Namibia and India. The sea of orange balls belonged to the blue alliance, which swept the floor with red and wrote the first loss into our record.

At home, an hour lasts sixty minutes, but at the FIRST Global Challenge the same unit of time lasts but a few blinks. Before the students could catch their breath, they were already standing in the queue in front of the big stage. Soon it was time for match 36, in which we stood shoulder to shoulder with Tajikistan and Spain. Together we managed to score 161 points in two minutes and thirty seconds, but it was not enough, so we shook hands with the blue alliance, our friends from El Salvador, the Cook Islands and Japan, who earned the win with 204 points.

The lunch break did us good, although we had to take it in shifts, since someone always had to be in the pit. Refreshed and with a few more smiles, the boys soon set about forging a strategy with their peers from Germany and Colombia. And so the blue alliance faced Great Britain, Bulgaria and Chile in match number 75. This time the referee pointed towards us, so we ran back to the pit with a 60 : 45 result and our first win in our pocket.

A slightly longer break allowed us to lend a hand to our friends from South Africa, who were having some trouble with their robot and its software. We also took some time to call on the Canadian team, who were competing with a scissor lift robot. We remember our own unsuccessful attempts with this mechanism back in Greece, and now they are experiencing it first-hand (well, on their own aluminium extrusions).

After the match, we were informed of a party that would take place after the dinner break. So, refreshed, we returned to the robot fields, where, with music from the opening DJ and some desserts for company, we awaited a secret guest. Black Eyed Peas music was spun by apl.de.ap, who drew every competitor to the front of the stage. Thus we built up enough weariness for an easy sleep, and after an hour of socialising, we headed back to the hotel. We dropped off our things, and some of us rested by working out the finer details of how the gadgets in the flat work, whilst others played Exploding Kittens late into the night.

Until next time

buenas noches

entry.title: A Guest of Honour at the Opening Ceremony
entry.summary: A new date on the calendar got us on our feet, through the plates of the breakfast room and out of the hotel to the robot venue. Repairs and upgrades to the robot soon followed, chiefly on the launcher and on the extension mechanism, which is meant to increase the capacity of the ball storage.
entry.content:
A new date on the calendar got us on our feet, through the plates of the breakfast room and out of the hotel to the robot venue. Repairs and upgrades to the robot soon followed, chiefly on the launcher and on the extension mechanism, which is meant to increase the capacity of the ball storage.

Those who had nothing to do at so early an hour chatted with the teams from South Africa and the Solomon Islands, and later saw to some intercultural networking over Cockta, a Slovenian fizzy drink. It turns out that foreigners are thrilled with its herbal extracts and find it strikingly different from other colas. The Slovak team linked the drink’s name to their word for stuttering (koktaš). Whilst we were mingling, we were also visited by Kelly, a Slovenian-American who has been a FIRST volunteer for a long time. Those Slovenian roots have clearly taken hold, as Kelly happily came back for more Cockta and later for Šumi sweets too.

We went to lunch with our friends from South Africa, swapping recipes and photographs of our everyday dishes (from Balkan delicacies to African desserts). After lunch, the students lent a hand to our friends from Norway, who still had a great deal of work ahead of them on their robot. Meanwhile, in the Slovenian pit, the balls were flying high enough for the robot to earn a green tick from its drivers. The mentors watched the balls from afar, as they were busy looking into what is new at XRP, who have developed 3D-printed robot arms this year.

Soon the clock in South Korea struck the hour for the boys of the Slovenian team to change into Vegova Ljubljana T-shirts and national costume, which, combined with custom-made seagrass hats, make up our traditional attire. Whilst we were waiting to be called into the queue for the parade of flags, we were visited by Ms Miriam Možgan, the Slovenian Ambassador to South Korea. We quickly made each other’s acquaintance and presented the robot and this year’s challenge. Then the students queued up in alphabetical order of countries, whilst the mentors accompanied the Ambassador to the stands to watch the opening ceremony. The waving of the flags of 185 nations was followed by a K-pop performance, a speech by the Mayor of Incheon with live speech recognition (and translation afterwards) and, of course, an address by Mr Dean Kamen.

The opening ceremony ended with a light-and-dance spectacle, in which the true artistry lay in the dancers’ costumes changing colour, the shifting backdrop on the screen and the synchronised choreography.

On the way out, we were handed Korean crisps, and we set off in search of dinner. With dinner behind us, we headed to a shopping centre that stays open until eleven o’clock at night, where besides a Lotte shop we also found a Toys R Us, parrots and axolotls, metal chopsticks, matcha ice cream and a vending machine full of mystery boxes.

When the lady from the shop kindly but firmly sent us on our way (‘bye bye’), we headed to Central Park, where we found the SONGDO sign along with Incheon’s mascots, temples, instruments, solar-powered cats, deer and various statues, all set around the calm water at the heart of the park.

After a long walk, a soft bed and a heated lavatory seat awaited us at the hotel.

Until next time,

noapte bună

entry.title: Inspecting Robots, Temples and Aeroplanes
entry.summary: We began a calm, foggy morning in Incheon’s Songdo district with an alarm clock, breakfast and a muster in the lobby. Today’s goal was to get the robot ready and test it, since it had to be taken apart to meet the luggage requirements. Once that is done, we still need the judges’ tick confirming that the robot is fit to compete. Into action!
entry.content:
We began a calm, foggy morning in Incheon’s Songdo district with an alarm clock, breakfast and a muster in the lobby. Today’s goal was to get the robot ready and test it, since it had to be taken apart to meet the luggage requirements. Once that is done, we still need the judges’ tick confirming that the robot is fit to compete. Into action!

After reassembling the robot, we found that the software we had put together was not working yet, as the ball launcher did not shoot high enough on the field and took too long to spin up. So we spent a while implementing motor speed control based on RPM.

Meanwhile, volunteers kept popping by to check whether we were ready for robot inspection, which we had to politely decline. In between, we treated ourselves to a break with a catered lunch on the first floor, outside the arena.

Afterwards, we went to have a look at the new parts that will be used next season, and we already cannot wait for the new geared motors, new extrusions, bearings and other goodies. Those who were not working on the robot visited other countries’ pits and got to know teams such as North Macedonia, Guam, American Samoa and others.

To make the most of the afternoon, we went over the software with our only programmer, whilst the others fine-tuned the secondary mechanisms for extending and picking up balls.

Over dinner, we drew up a plan for an evening stroll. So, after a sufficient amount of chicken and salmon, we dropped our things off at the hotel, changed and hopped on a bus. A walk up the hill took us past a statue of legs on a roof and a ‘Have a wonderful time’ sign and, as the view of the city opened up, brought us to Heungnyunsa temple. In silence, we walked past little dragon statues and up the steps to a golden tower, from where we could see the city in the distance. Next to it we found an elephant statue, and at the top of the hill, places for prayer, some of them even set into the rock face or a small cave.

Then we zoomed out on Google Maps and discovered some sort of museum nearby, so we marched off in that direction and came upon an open-air museum about the American landing at Incheon. We got to see tanks, fighter jets, watchtowers with searchlights, a tower dedicated to the soldiers and, in the wooded part of the exhibition, a few more aeroplanes and ships. Before taking our leave, we also discovered postcards and an aquarium projection on the wall next to the entrance.

We ended the evening stroll by marching to a bus stop closer to the sea, passing a karaoke bar and a shop on the way, where we stopped to try some new juices. The bus took us safely home, and all that was left after that was sleep.

Until next time,

laku noć

entry.title: Good Luck Getting to Seoul
entry.summary: Landing with LOT moved our clocks seven hours forward. At the airport, we happily showed our documents and faces and left our fingerprints to enter the country. We found our suitcases quickly, one of them even sporting a special yellow lock, which means it has to be opened and the tools inside it explained.
entry.content:
Landing with LOT moved our clocks seven hours forward. At the airport, we happily showed our documents and faces and left our fingerprints to enter the country. We found our suitcases quickly, one of them even sporting a special yellow lock, which means it has to be opened and the tools inside it explained.

Instead of one of the suitcases, we simply received a note in a plastic crate asking the owner to report to the returns window. Our first impressions were rather odd, as the people there (the staff!) had no idea where this miraculous window was supposed to be. The solution lay in a huge screen through which we reached an operator, who knew to send us to the LOT window. There, a filled-in form was followed by a polite thank-you and the assurance that within 24 hours the suitcase would already be very close.

A walk through the airport showed us little islands of plants, a neatly kept space, unfamiliar shops and more besides. After some more searching, we managed to find the welcome desk for robotics Olympians such as ourselves. We waited a little longer, crossed at a traffic light with huge numbers and kerbs in matching colours, and boarded a coach with motorised leg rests. Pleasantly surprised, we rode to the Oakwood Premier hotel in Incheon, the city closest to the airport.

On the way, we saw huge bridges, a clear dominance of Hyundai and Kia cars, great tower blocks and cargo ships sailing into port. The coach dropped us off in front of a 305-metre-tall building of 65 storeys. We left our luggage, since there were still three hours until check-in, and set out to explore the area around the hotel. Our first stop was the shops across the road, where we found a selection of restaurants and the convenience store Nice to CU, where we went for juices and snacks. We quickly realised that trying new things here would be quite the adventure: neither the corn juice nor the grain juice deserved any praise, and the dried octopus pieces were rather a chewing challenge. The juices made from fruits we know, however, did not disappoint. We were surprised that when paying by card, one has to leave a signature on a small graphics tablet.

Afterwards, we met up with Jaka, a former team member and mentor who once again came to help run the event as a volunteer this year. We made our way to the Hakoya ramen restaurant, where we ran into the mentors of the Croatian team. We were given a sound piece of advice: if the gentleman says it is only a little spicy, do not believe him. When the huge bowls landed in front of us, together with side dishes of a special kind of ginger, we did not speak for a few minutes and simply savoured the flavours.

Before leaving, we asked the gentleman whether he had any advice on how to get to Seoul, which is actually smaller than Incheon by area but is the capital and the most populous city. He told us exactly which bus to take, whilst Jaka explained how paying for bus and metro journeys works. So we went to get an EZL transport card, which Android phone owners must use, whereas Apple enthusiasts are a little more privileged, as all they need is the T-Money app.

At reception, we received the key cards for two rooms in the five-star hotel, with the students lodged on the 48th floor and the two mentors at a suitable distance on the 55th.

As today, Monday, was our only free day, we headed to the Incheon the Sharp First World bus stop, boarded bus M6450 and set off for Seoul’s Gangnam district. The communication difficulties did not stop at the alphabet: explaining that we wished to pay for several people with one card kept the driver busy for a few stops. A good hour’s journey brought us to a city of 10 million people.

We continued on foot to an electronics market, and by the time we arrived, we already had a feel for Seoul’s streets, full of restaurants and all manner of shops. The 11-storey building full of stalls mostly offered figures of animated characters, some old audio electronics, video games and the like. We were not browsing the stalls alone, as plenty of teenagers were there with us, hoping to find a collector’s item.

We concluded our wanderings at the Lotte shop on the ground floor, where we picked up snacks and drinks and headed for our next destination, the statue dedicated to the Gangnam Style dance. We soon came to appreciate the size of Slovenia and its towns, as what looked like a short walk turned out to be rather longer than we would have liked. Apparently, Google Maps has not been in South Korea for very long, so it cannot estimate walking times between two points. And so we walked a good 10 km, taking in all the unusual signs, restaurants and rubbish bins along the way.

We discovered that Koreans are mad about tennis and golf, as they have dedicated shops, especially for the latter (e.g. Nike Golf). Another thing that surprised us on our walk was the number of high-end cars parked in front of random restaurants and pubs on random streets.

We finally made it across every last pedestrian crossing and, on the way to the COEX shopping centre, enjoyed wide pavements with scarcely anyone on them. The hardest part was finding the entrance to the shopping centre, so we ended up going in through the underpass of the hotel next door. Inside, we came across all sorts of shops and restaurants, but our aim was to see a special space that looks like a library.

With closing time fast approaching, we found the exit and walked along the main road to the Gangnam Style statue, where they have kindly set up a screen that plays PSY’s once wildly popular song.

The night was still young, so we made the most of it and also visited Bongeunsa, the Buddhist temple across the road, where we walked uphill in complete silence and took in the sacred site. We got a great deal more than we expected: after passing the prayer halls, we were greeted at the top by a huge, beautifully lit monument.

All that remained was to catch the bus back. We settled in comfortably at the right stop, and a few minutes before the bus was due, we spotted one of the first English signs we had seen, saying that the bus would stop on the opposite side of the road. We hurried over, caught the green man and, with about two minutes to spare, settled comfortably onto the bus. This time, we simply showed the driver a translation of ‘five people’, and everything went as it should. Apparently, Koreans show the number five with one hand differently (instead of five outstretched fingers, a closed fist with the thumb sticking out). On the way back, we could feel the difference in comfort between an electric and an ordinary bus.

Longing for some rest, we returned to the hotel, unpacked, put the souvenirs we had bought on the shelf and went to bed.

Until next time,

annyeonghi jumuseyo

entry.title: Korea at Last!
entry.summary: The clock struck morning on Sunday 4 October 2026. We gathered at the Zavod 404 workshop, loaded the robot and our luggage into a van and a car, and set off for Zagreb Airport. A good hour’s drive later, we were already wrapping the robot box and our suitcases in cling film. We then took the box two floors down for the oversized baggage check.
entry.content:
The clock struck morning on Sunday 4 October 2026. We gathered at the Zavod 404 workshop, loaded the robot and our luggage into a van and a car, and set off for Zagreb Airport. A good hour’s drive later, we were already wrapping the robot box and our suitcases in cling film. We then took the box two floors down for the oversized baggage check.

Bag drop went smoothly, whilst at the security check we received the questions we had expected about the robot’s batteries and the tape (‘Šta će ti ovo?’ – ‘What do you need this for?’). We then hurried to our gate, stood about for a couple of minutes and, quite without meaning to, ended up at the front of the queue. We boarded the aeroplane to Warsaw, and our journey to the FIRST Global Challenge, the Olympics of robotics, had truly begun. On the way, we snacked on spinach and apple turnovers. During the flight, we had the opportunity to observe young air steward Tim, who kept blocking the aisle. In the end, he decided that one is only young once and wished to find out what the armrests tasted like, which his mum actively prevented (‘Tim, you can lick Mummy, but not the aeroplane’).

Before long, we landed on Polish soil, where people are fond of bringing up beavers. We had about 50 minutes for our connection, so we lengthened our stride and made the next boarding. In the queue, we also bumped into our friends from Norway, who had a new team line-up. On board, we had the privilege of listening to Chopin, watching films or lying awake thanks to a crying baby. We could prepare our taste buds for Korean food, as both dinner and breakfast were meat with noodles, side dishes (kimchi, octopus) and fruit. We shall write again once we land in South Korea, which is 10 hours and 30 minutes from now.

Until next time,

lahko noč

entry.title: A Coconut, Then Home
entry.summary: Some of us began the morning of the last day earlier than others. Anyone who wished had the chance to go to the all-night shop one last time that week; otherwise there remained the option of a lie-in and a later breakfast. In the shop we found snacks and drinks, and a coconut, which the owner opened for us with a knife, offering us a straw.
entry.content:
Some of us began the morning of the last day earlier than others. Anyone who wished had the chance to go to the all-night shop one last time that week; otherwise there remained the option of a lie-in and a later breakfast. In the shop we found snacks and drinks, and a coconut, which the owner opened for us with a knife, offering us a straw.

The shops in Panama were operating normally even though it was Sunday, though each had its own opening hours. So we three musketeers set off for the Arrecha shop, which we already knew, did our shopping in a hurry and went back to the hotel. We collected our things and gathered in the hotel lobby. The coach soon arrived for team ‘Slovenia’. We handed our things to the driver to load into the coach’s hold. At the airport we immediately stepped aside and redistributed our things amongst the suitcases, also stowing in them the contents of the bags that some had forgotten to pack.

With our suitcases ready and weighed, we joined a long queue. Halfway along it, a gentleman came up to us and offered to take us to the other side of the hall, where the queue was empty. We seized the opportunity and followed. On the way we were told that we had to wrap the robot’s box in plastic film. The team went on ahead, and a mentor approached the man with the wrapping machine. Whilst loading the box, the mentor noticed that the machine issued receipts and asked the price. The chap pointed to a sign reading ‘17$’, which the mentor politely declined. We then checked whether we could wrap the box ourselves, and they said that we could. So we applied silver duct tape along the edges, round the corners and over the heads of the screws. We checked in between, and each time the answer was ‘a little more’. Then, by a slightly roundabout route, we got past the staff on the grounds that ‘your colleague said it was OK’. At the check-in desk, the mentor was handed a slip to sign and tick, confirming that the luggage was being checked in unwrapped. And so that complication was resolved. Now for security and the aeroplane. We waited for a while at the original gate and wandered round the shops. Meanwhile the gate was changed, so we slowly moved to the other end of the corridor, but there a long queue and another security check awaited us (aha, so that is why we had been told we could not take drinks from the shops onto the aeroplane).

A delay of almost an hour was followed by the journey to Miami airport. Because of the delay, we arrived late into a queue with 100–200 other people without American citizenship. After briefly making our case for entry and having our photographs taken, we went to collect our luggage and dashed to our gate. When we got there, however, we were told that boarding for this flight had closed. Fortunately we were all wearing straw hats, and they grasped that they were refusing boarding to seven people. They urgently called their superiors, and at some point one lady gave her colleague a 👍. Quickly, as if on a conveyor belt, we all checked in and dashed to security. A complication with the robot’s batteries was quickly resolved, and we hurried on, reached the gate and even waited in the queue for boarding. We settled calmly onto the aeroplane to Munich, where, after landing, we spent about 8 hours.

Until next time,

oíche mhaith

entry.title: Have You Got Any Souvenirs?
entry.summary: Three matches await us today, so we started early with the first match of the day, which the organisers list as number 299. This time we graced the red side together with the teams from the United Republic of Tanzania and the Czech Republic. The upgrades to the robot and a good strategy paid off, and we managed to conjure up a 74:68 result in our favour. This time, after two and a half minutes, we shook hands with the representatives of San Marino, the Netherlands and Latvia.
entry.content:
Three matches await us today, so we started early with the first match of the day, which the organisers list as number 299. This time we graced the red side together with the teams from the United Republic of Tanzania and the Czech Republic. The upgrades to the robot and a good strategy paid off, and we managed to conjure up a 74:68 result in our favour. This time, after two and a half minutes, we shook hands with the representatives of San Marino, the Netherlands and Latvia.

A short pause, and we were already rushing back into the queue. This time we were paired with our neighbours and could get closer to the Italians, and the trio was completed by the representatives of Afghanistan. The match on field 4 was tense, but sadly match no. 317 ended in victory for our colleagues from Djibouti, Cyprus and the Congo (36:40).

To round off the programme, we took part in qualification match number 337 on field 1. This time we had the honour of shaping the strategy and the match together with Nicaragua and Kyrgyzstan. We ended our attempt at the FIRST Global Challenge with a victory against (or rather with, since we wish to win as a community) Mozambique (who fielded only a human player – there were no drivers and no robot), Paraguay and Aruba. The final figures on the screen read 48:40. With that, Slovenia’s record stood at 8 wins, 2 draws and 2 defeats.

The end of the event was drawing near, so we had to start packing up the pit. Before setting about it, we made sure to have our photograph taken in our sponsors’ T-shirts.

Whilst we were packing up, visitors from other countries called by, asked us to sign their booklets and shirts, and asked whether we had any souvenirs left. The conversations drifted into presentations about Slovenia and vice versa, so now we know more about South Africa, Algeria, Ukraine and a few others. When we needed a rest, we went off to swap shirt for shirt with friendly countries.

At dinner we ate our fill, and after many burgers there were many boxes left over, so our students set off on a mission to build a tower. When it collapsed, they decided to reinforce the structure into a triangular prism. Before long, the building of the tower block encouraged other countries to contribute their boxes. Soon our colleagues from Moldova jumped in and helped with the tower enthusiastically. After three iterations, we found together the ideal structure, which resembled Dubai’s Burj Khalifa. One shoulder-stand later, we stood at the height of many boxes and received applause from the hall, as well as the watchful looks and smiles of the waiting staff. The tower then collapsed, of course, but no matter.

With the robot packed and the pit cleared, we made our way to the coach and back to the hotel. We devoted just under an hour to packing our luggage and securing the robot.

For a rest from packing, we ordered 2 Ubers and set off for the old town, Casco Viejo. The darkness of night was adorned by pleasant yellow lights, which accompanied us from our very first stop, the Plaza Herrera park. There we could look at monuments and buildings and catch one of the souvenir shops still open.

Carrier bags in hand, we continued to the end of the peninsula, where besides the sea we found monuments, a tower and a small stretch of wall.

A tunnel of lights escorted us back into town, after which we turned left into the street of hats, where we also found a hat shop.

Our way along narrow pavements and past armed police officers guarding the squares led us to the art museum, a church and the national theatre.

On the way back we also visited the church and the buildings on Independence Square (Plaza de la Independencia).

After that, with wet hair, we got into an Uber, which we had to order to the street next to the square (on account of the police), and went home.

Until next time,

dobroyi nochi

entry.title: A Celebration for a New Mechanism
entry.summary: A new day, new chances of success. After the morning ritual we dashed to the pit, where we finished the prototype of a new arm mechanism and also put it into service during the first qualification matches of the second day of the official competition.
entry.content:
A new day, new chances of success. After the morning ritual we dashed to the pit, where we finished the prototype of a new arm mechanism and also put it into service during the first qualification matches of the second day of the official competition.

The difference is that this time, instead of servo motors, we used Core Hex motors with gearing, as these motors are more robust. Soon the first opportunity arose to test them outside the pit and the practice fields. We played the first match of the day together with the Virgin Islands and India. The improvement to the arms quickly proved its worth, as we managed to collect more points than ever before and bring a 44:42 win back to the pit. Our colleagues on the opposite side of the field represented Israel, Guyana and Malta.

Match number 181 came round quickly, and we dashed off with the robot on its box to the queue for official matches. This time we graced the red alliance in the company of Bermuda and Kosovo. This time there was no better alliance, only equals: both our alliance and that of Eritrea, Luxembourg and Turkey took home 57 points.

The day granted us no long breaks – at most enough for a snack from another country, or a stroll and a chat. Soon the sound of the horn rang out on field 3, announcing the start of match 206. This time we were on the blue side together with Bulgaria and Korea. For the best possible result, we cooperated with our ‘opponents’, this time Syria, Saudi Arabia and Switzerland. Another win for us, 48:45. Slovenia’s record currently stands at 4 wins, 2 draws and 1 defeat.

We are drawing near the headline match on the schedule, but we are not quite there yet. Match number 232 still stands in between, in which we stood alongside São Tomé and Príncipe and Eswatini. We managed to raise our average a little further with a winning result of 58:56 against the United Arab Emirates, the Cook Islands and Benin.

The hour had come for the headline match on the headline field. This time, on field 5, we were paired with a couple of ‘giants’. Supporting us were the representatives of Kazakhstan and the United States of America, so we had our strategy ready and felt good before the match. On the opposite side we could look our colleagues from Venezuela, Papua New Guinea and Brunei Darussalam in the eye. This time, amongst the ‘giants’, we were the bigger ones, and we took home a pleasant boost to our average with a result of 114:98.

The strenuous day was followed by dinner in a somewhat roomier hall than before. During lunch we had noticed them moving tables and setting up a stage, so we deduced that there would be a party that day, a conclusion only reinforced by the array of party accessories on the tables. We could help ourselves to bracelets, glasses or sticks, all with lights for the dark.

Towards the end of dinner a DJ began to play music, the bass growing more noticeable by the minute. Soon the lights went out, and the students hurried to the dance floor below the stage. The flashing of glow sticks and glasses, the loud music and the jumping of young roboticists shook the floor throughout the hall.

After the guest DJ’s opening set, Mr Dean Kamen paid us a visit, cheerfully announced that two countries held up by the weather had arrived, and proposed moving them into the final pool of 32 countries so that they could play. Naturally, the whole dance floor agreed. Then came the announcement of a special guest, who truly got the evening going. Out in front of us stepped will.i.am and performed live, making for an unforgettable evening. On the way home we scrambled to secure ourselves a Soyo transport coach, which likes to keep the party going all the way to the hotel. Latin American songs and deep bass make the journey shorter.

Until next time,

bari gisher

entry.title: Even the Lizards Get the Joke
entry.summary: A hearty breakfast to start the new day was swiftly followed by boarding the coach. The sun shone on the road, the slits in the bridge and the hill with the Panamanian flag, where sloths and parrots hide. Should one wish to see butterflies and frogs as well, however, one would have to drive some 45 minutes out of the city (or so the wide world of the internet tells us).
entry.content:
A hearty breakfast to start the new day was swiftly followed by boarding the coach. The sun shone on the road, the slits in the bridge and the hill with the Panamanian flag, where sloths and parrots hide. Should one wish to see butterflies and frogs as well, however, one would have to drive some 45 minutes out of the city (or so the wide world of the internet tells us).

In the entrance hall many competitors were waiting, ready to enter the pits. We turned the queue to our advantage and popped over to a viewpoint by the water to gaze our fill at the shipping. We carried on along the footpath to while away some time, until the excessive heat of the Panamanian weather began to drive us back.

On the way back to the competition area, our eye was caught by an unusual combination of colours, followed by a tail. We had found an iguana basking in the sun. We greeted it politely, photographed it and tested its knowledge of engineering jokes. At the joke it nodded kindly, but when it had had enough of our jokes, it set off in the direction of the z-axis (vertically), up a tree.

Having parked ourselves on the sofa and the fishing chair, we made the last repairs to the robot and so prepared ourselves for the first ranked matches. The boys still had some time before the qualification matches began, so, having got hold of the match schedule, they decided to lend a hand to their first teammates – the Federated States of Micronesia. Their mechanism for using the accelerator (a component of the playing field) was not working at its best, you see, so the boys stepped in with parts and a design to help them build it. During the process another country came to help as well, which left our boys free to take a stroll around the alphabet of colourful flags.

Owing to the uniqueness and efficiency of their chassis, the boys entered the so-called Skills Challenge, in which the entered teams (each separately) show off their robot’s capabilities in a somewhat different way (collecting and transporting balls against the clock, and shooting or throwing them). During the challenge certain imperfections in the robot came to light, but the boys were not sure what exactly might be causing the robot to behave in this way.

The first matches soon began, and with them some harsh discoveries. Match number 30, in which we had the Federated States of Micronesia and Taiwan at our side, was poor in terms of points, but it gave us a view of the robot’s real condition. We won this match by a whisker, 21:18, against the blue alliance, formed by Japan, Ukraine and Serbia. During the match we confirmed the problem – the servo motors for the arm mechanism were not durable enough. So far we had destroyed, on average, one servo motor per practice or qualification match. We were aware that we did not have enough time to replace the whole mechanism, so for the time being we serviced it as we went and manoeuvred with care.

We livened up the second match of the day on the first field (of five) in the arena. This time we were paired with Denmark and Ghana in the blue alliance. The unreliability of the arms could be felt in the points, as we finished this match with a score of 25:22. The winners’ applause for match number 49 went to our half of the field, after which we shook hands with our colleagues from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mauritania and Guatemala and made our way out of the arena.

During the third match of the first day we discovered a new flaw in our robot. Whilst playing with our colleagues from Estonia and Pakistan, we noticed that the robot was moving more slowly than it should, which bothered both drivers, as our robot is primarily intended to play a supporting role. This time fortune kept its teeth hidden, though not entirely. Match number 76 ended 28:28, so the applause was shared out evenly between us and the red alliance, made up this time of our peers from Malawi, Kiribati and China.

The last match of the first day of the olympiad’s competitive part was assigned number 96. Our path led us to an appearance on the main field (number 5). This time we represented the blue alliance together with Belarus and the Gambia. Stress, weariness and much else besides could be blamed for the outcome of the match, but it is also only fair to shake the hand of a better opponent. This time the winning score of 26:22 fell to Panama, the Maldives and Armenia.

Whilst waiting for dinner, we took time to reflect and realised that this match could have had a different outcome had our colleagues from Belarus not pinched our hanging rope, which cost us a few points. We also confirmed that the battery was draining too quickly in normal operation, which could point to resistance in one of the motors or wheels. We quickly located and replaced the troublesome part and repaired the assembly it belonged to. Besides this, we set about making a prototype of a new arm mechanism. Time overtook us, and so we went off to dinner in our culture’s attire (in our case, straw hats).

The students were in the company of their peers, whilst the two mentors talked with Michael, who works as an engineer at Boeing. We endured a long queue, but this time the helpings were more generous for it. In the meantime we had a visit (and an address) from the founder, Mr Dean Kamen, who in the course of the speech introduced a new guest – the famous chef Paul Irvyne. We were told in confidence that next year at the event we would have the chance to taste cooking from other, more famous hands. The evening continued with conga lines, team photographs and the printing of pictures.

On returning home we arranged a visit to a new shop in the immediate vicinity of the Hotel Megapolis. We dashed to the other side of the main road, sacrificing a few minutes on a detour to get across, as pedestrian crossings on the main road are rare. The Arrecha shop was advertised as a chemist’s, but inside (judging by its wares) it resembled a Pepco. We wandered about for quite some time and stepped out with LEGO bricks, snacks, soft toys and whatnot. Curiosity and a surplus of energy led us on a lap of new territory. We walked along a new road and witnessed a somewhat more realistic picture of the city, one that includes rather more rubbish. Soon we found ourselves in a park with a playground, and next to both we also found the Pacific.

Curiosity led us to a nearby pier, and on the way a surprise awaited us. Round the corner, in the dark, two police officers with a motorcycle were waiting for us. They asked us in Spanish where we were going; we guessed the context, and one of the mentors said ‘foto’ and pointed at the pier. They wished to see our papers, which was no problem until it turned out that one member had no papers to hand and one mentor did not look the same as in the photograph (which we resolved by lifting a lock of hair). They asked how long we would be there (‘tempo?’), to which we replied by holding up five fingers. We hurried to the pier, which was whole at first, then collapsed in the middle, then whole again. We had neither the time nor the desire to clamber over the collapsed pier, so instead we devoted a minute or so to taking photographs. On the way back to the hotel we were kindly reminded that in this part of the world hooting is a friendly warning and very probably a breach of the traffic regulations. Soon we found ourselves back in our hotel beds, waiting with closed eyes for a new day.

Until next time,

mačka omáčka

entry.title: Palms, a Canal and a Parade
entry.summary: We began the third day of our American adventure in the same way, except that today we had to make sure that the suitcase with our national costumes boarded the coach with us after breakfast. We set off through the sunny morning, once again over the bridge and through traffic full of precautionary hooting to warn of merging.
entry.content:
We began the third day of our American adventure in the same way, except that today we had to make sure that the suitcase with our national costumes boarded the coach with us after breakfast. We set off through the sunny morning, once again over the bridge and through traffic full of precautionary hooting to warn of merging.

The first item of the day was the final arrangement of things in the pit, which meant trying out the fishing chair and inflating the ‘sofa’, which later proved a real hit, delighting every visitor.

On the programme for the day was testing the robot in friendly matches (practice matches), for which the members had to sign up in advance. Whilst waiting for the warm-up matches, the boys tested the robot right there in the aisle between the pits. When the boys did not have their hands full, they went round looking at robots, trying sweets or attending to various social duties (signing booklets, flags and the like).

Hard work deserves proper rest too, so the crew also went off to see the surrounding area. Across the road was a path that led us to a monument relating to South Korea and Panama. A little beyond this monument lies the water that flows through the Panama Canal. Just then a large cargo ship crossed our field of view, heading towards the famous bridge.

Closer to the bridge we also found a small jetty, on which workers were loading cargo in smaller lots onto smaller boats. The surroundings had been adorned the whole way by varied vegetation, from palms to cacti, from colourful birds and flowers to the untidy wiring of missing street lamps.

Soon the moment came when the boys had to put down their tools, park the robot and go to dinner, where they met long queues and food that kept running out. After a somewhat less plentiful dinner, they put on their costumes and hats and went off to the dress rehearsal. Its end was followed by a short rest and time to freshen up, and shortly afterwards the line of flags was already forming.

The two mentors took their places at the end of a cluster of people already diligently warming the tin stands. It was there that we two mentors met our colleague Gregory, a student back at the competition in Dubai (2019), and impressed our old friend with our memory, as we remembered that year’s entire line-up. What gave the game away was hearing that Gregory was from Venezuela.

The marching and the waving of flags in the hands of future innovators were accompanied by applause from the audience and now and then by a few trumpets, depending on how many visitors had come from the country in question. The sea of flags heralded the start of the speeches by the founder of FIRST, the First Lady of Panama and several other important guests. The premiere of a new piece of music for the FGC competition was followed by a true Panamanian carnival, in which a choir and an orchestra provided the musical accompaniment for the dancers. They were dressed in traditional costumes of varying splendour.

Tired but happy, we took our seats on the coach home. Some of us had a quiet journey home, whilst the seats of others shook to the rhythm of the bass from Latin songs. At the hotel we put down our things and headed to McDonald’s and afterwards to our friend at the 24/7 shop, on the way to which we encountered an American speciality – a Cybertruck.

In the shop we bought various drinks, teas, snacks, soft-toy toucans and magnets. As part of the cultural experience we also tried a plantain (a broad banana that smells of cucumber), which we prepared according to a traditional recipe.

Until next time,

god natt

entry.title: New Colours and Raccoons on the Beach
entry.summary: A few hours’ sleep and a sunny morning were enough for us to recover from the long flight. At twenty past six, local time, we met on the second floor and went to breakfast. Fresh fruit, ćevapi and other more typical hotel fare managed to fortify us, together with exotic juices (passion fruit, jugo and so on). The clock ticked quickly that morning, as we had to be on the coach by seven o’clock. We gathered our things, drank in the sunrise and, after a long wait for the lift, brought the robot down from the 24th floor (of 62) to the lobby.
entry.content:
A few hours’ sleep and a sunny morning were enough for us to recover from the long flight. At twenty past six, local time, we met on the second floor and went to breakfast. Fresh fruit, ćevapi and other more typical hotel fare managed to fortify us, together with exotic juices (passion fruit, jugo and so on). The clock ticked quickly that morning, as we had to be on the coach by seven o’clock. We gathered our things, drank in the sunrise and, after a long wait for the lift, brought the robot down from the 24th floor (of 62) to the lobby.

The journey to this year’s venue passed quickly, as we could enjoy the view of the sea and the tall buildings, whilst languages from other continents flew into each ear. The Panama Convention Center welcomed us with tropical vegetation and a train in front of the entrance. On our arrival, the large white glass foyer was sheltering many teenagers from the muggy air of the host country, and they managed to break the monotony with socialising, music and dancing. As in many a year, the fun was led by students from Venezuela and Tunisia, so boredom was at the very bottom of the register. Our team parked itself to one side and gave the students free rein to get to know their peers. Soon the organisers directed us to the right of the entrance, towards the door of the hall in which we would be spending the next few days together. The queue grew ever longer, but in a herd, straw hats are easy to count.

We quickly managed to locate our pit and immediately set about the traditional decorating. Half the team hung up little flags, whilst the other half unpacked the robot and set about servicing and testing it.

The rest of our time at the event was taken up with testing the robot on the field, getting to know new friends, tasting new sweets, catching up with old colleagues and spending time together as a team over lunch and dinner.

On arriving at the hotel, we took a few minutes to rest and then met in the hotel lobby, from where we set out. We stopped across the road at an outlet shopping centre, where we found a great deal of everything in the Wow shop. Our shopping ended at the till with a camping chair, an inflatable chair, sugary drinks and a 10 kW loudspeaker on the conveyor belt. So as not to walk about the city with our purchases, we called briefly at our hotel rooms, where we tried out the chair and carefully read the loudspeaker’s instructions for use, which were questionable but acceptable.

Soon we set off again with the aim of reaching the sea and visiting the raccoons. Our route took us along the main road that runs parallel to the shore. As we walked, we saw quite a few lowered taxis and cars with blue or yellow headlamps. This time the pedestrian crossings were kind to us, and their buttons worked as they should. Crossings over the main road are very rare, and their purpose is to let pedestrians reach the island in the middle of the main road. The island holds a car park and a red bridge, by which one can cross another pair of lanes of the main road to reach the shore.

Walking along the shore, we met many runners and narrow benches on the broad path. Alongside our route ran a path for roller skaters and cyclists as well. On the way to the raccoons we passed a few playgrounds, a UV light meter and a few drinking fountains. The water in Panama has not, so far, been the tastiest. Soon our attention was caught by cats sleeping on the sea wall. Behind them we saw glinting eyes with little hands close by. Behind the cats were three raccoons on the rocks by the beach. We soon gave up on photographing them, as they were hidden in the dark of the night. A little later, however, we came across a new foursome of raccoons. They cheerfully approached us in the hope that we would offer them supper. When they realised that nothing would come of it, they made for a nearby litter bin to try their luck. It was then that we realised how nimble they are at climbing, into bins and up trees alike. In the process one of the raccoons found itself on the other side of a fence (we know not how) and could not work out how to get out of the children’s playground. For a while it struggled with the fence, but it could not climb over it. We soon went to help and guided it out, whereupon it showed the finest grasp of an orthonormal 3D basis. Having escorted them home (to the wall by the beach), we set off home ourselves, and on the way our attention was caught by an unknown species of bird resembling a swallow. As very amateur biologists, we analysed it and soon gave up on our research.

Our way home took us back along the other side of the road, from where we later rejoined a route the two mentors knew, back to the Hotel Megapolis.

Back at the hotel, we devoted a few minutes to planning the next day and then all retired to our quarters. Tomorrow some more work on the robot and the opening ceremony await us, so energy will be most welcome.

Until next time,

Gudnaet bae mi go fo slip

entry.title: Welcome to the Land of Orchids!
entry.summary: This year’s team began its journey on 27 October 2025 at five o’clock in the morning at Brnik. Repacking and weighing the luggage was followed by the logistics of checking in the robot as a piece of luggage. Once we had our boarding cards in hand, we went through security and headed for the gate of our flight, where we could allow ourselves a few minutes to rest and look at the aeroplanes.
entry.content:
This year’s team began its journey on 27 October 2025 at five o’clock in the morning at Brnik. Repacking and weighing the luggage was followed by the logistics of checking in the robot as a piece of luggage. Once we had our boarding cards in hand, we went through security and headed for the gate of our flight, where we could allow ourselves a few minutes to rest and look at the aeroplanes.

The flight to Frankfurt took about two hours, and after landing we quickly dealt with the travel logistics and parked ourselves in front of the next gate. We spent the rest of the time finding and enjoying a snack, or playing skateboarding games on the airport’s consoles.

Our departure from Frankfurt was not difficult, though we were split between the upper and lower decks of the aeroplane. We settled in comfortably, set our hats in our laps or hung them on a hook, and passed the time sleeping, attending to work duties or watching films. The 10-hour flight passed without trouble, though it lasted only 4 hours (if one looked only at the times of departure and arrival).

Landing in Florida treated us to a view of densely built-up suburbs, swimming pools and American ‘highways’. As we did not have American passports, we were directed into a long queue, at the end of which a short interrogation awaited us, along with the taking of our fingerprints (4 on each hand and the thumb of each hand). Shortly before our turn came, we spotted a notice on a screen saying that we were not allowed to bring in food, so we had to eat our chocolate bars and sandwiches in a hurry (as it turned out, there was no trouble after all, but at least not all of us were hungry afterwards). Next came check-in, where we lost some time owing to language barriers, and still more time slipped away because, with our last member, they misunderstood the situation and thought a visa was needed for entry (despite our ESTAs being in order). Consequently we dashed to security, where, as luck would have it, they searched several of our rucksacks, so that we reached boarding at the very last second. We had a few minutes to rest, but not enough for the hungry members to find somewhere selling food. The team members did, however, manage to record a piece for the Social Media Challenge, in which they had to document their journey to Panama.

At the last second we learnt that boarding cards were not enough and that we had to go through the check-in procedure with our passports and ESTAs. At last we got onto the aeroplane, took up our positions and surrendered ourselves to the sunset and tropical juices (guava and pineapple, amongst others).

When we arrived in Panama, we met a lady with a ‘FIRST Global’ sign, who walked us across to the other side of the airport (literally) on foot to go through the immigration inspection, where they likewise took our fingerprints and a photograph. Then we had our photograph taken by the Panamanian flag, collected our luggage and made for the exit, where we were shown onto a coach with a Turkish interior (carpets and wallpaper).

The journey took us and the teams of South Korea and Ecuador past buses with flashing lights on their roofs, along motorways and past blocks of flats to the pleasantly illuminated city. In the lobby of the Hotel Megapolis we met several more teams waiting for their rooms. Evidently the logistics of the rooms had become rather complicated, as every team spent some 30 minutes at reception before receiving rooms, which were becoming available as they went along. After an hour and a half of waiting, our turn came, and we two mentors slowly filled in the details and waited for rooms to become available, whilst the other teams complained. The procedure was long, admittedly, but the real problem was weariness and the late hour.

Having successfully moved into our rooms, we finished the technical documentation and took a walk to a nearby shop. On the walk, the two of us discovered that the city really is safe (as the gentleman at passport control in Miami had hinted). Every 200 metres, you see, we met a security guard or a police officer, whereas on the whole walk we did not meet 10 people altogether in a good half-hour. The day ended with a gentleman in the Marbella shop, who spoke neither Spanish nor English, managing to rewire the card machine so that we could buy instant noodles without entering the shop. ‘Muchos gracias’ rounded off the experience (and awakened a desire for the drink ‘pipa fria’) and set us on our way back to the flat, where, with the help of a kettle, we boiled water and ate our noodles at half past one in the morning, Panama time. As for how we function on just under four hours’ sleep, you may read about that in the next post.

Until next time,

buenas noches

entry.title: ‘Would You Sign My Shirt?’
entry.summary: The penultimate day of September had arrived, and with it the last day of the FIRST Global Challenge competition for 2024. The morning ritual was followed by yet more servicing of the robot, as we wished to finish the competition in winning style. Two matches lay ahead of us, which meant that we had the chance to toil away until about half past twelve and then have the rest of the day at the stadium free.
entry.content:
The penultimate day of September had arrived, and with it the last day of the FIRST Global Challenge competition for 2024. The morning ritual was followed by yet more servicing of the robot, as we wished to finish the competition in winning style. Two matches lay ahead of us, which meant that we had the chance to toil away until about half past twelve and then have the rest of the day at the stadium free.

The repairs were nearly complete, but before they were finished came match number 307, which we played alongside Kiribati and San Marino. The opposite (red) half of the field was graced by the representatives of Serbia, the Bahamas and Syria. Victory slipped from our grasp by a hair’s breadth, and so we conceded defeat, 59–55.

‘We have more than an hour until the next match!’ we told ourselves, and carried on with the sorely needed repairs. Soon the robot could stand on its own two feet again, but we changed our strategy so as not to go for the highest baskets, as we did not wish to risk anything else breaking. And so the siren soon sounded for the start of match number 335. The blue alliance comprised Slovenia, Spain – whose robot had the same mechanism as ours – and Latvia. On the other side we could see the colours of Puerto Rico, Switzerland and Kosovo. We won the last match of the olympiad by a resounding 139–119. This last victory made up for all our past defeats and put smiles on our students’ faces.

The end of the regular programme was followed by lunch and then the announcement of the top 24 teams and 8 random ones, all of which would be mixed together into alliances of four to battle for a place in the finals. The game would still be played three against three, but each of the four countries in an alliance would have to appear on the field at least once. For the play-offs and finals, however, the rules of the game were somewhat different and thus more demanding – 3 extra blue balls were added at precisely specified positions, which can make extra points possible. We were not called amongst the best 32, so we could treat ourselves to a rest.

For our team, the rest of the day consisted of signing our fellow competitors’ shirts, watching matches and cheering on the Norwegians, who had been selected for the elimination rounds. Our friends from the north soon met with bad luck, however, as one of the robots in their alliance ran into trouble, and so they lost their matches and with them the chance of appearing in the finals. Whilst the students cheered and watched the matches, the two mentors stood guard over the pit and signed more shirts and booklets.

When the team returned to its workspace, we had the chance to swap shirts with our neighbours from Slovakia, as each of us had received 3 shirts. We also cheerfully handed out T-shirts bearing the words ‘Ljubljana je najlepše mesto’ (‘Ljubljana is the most beautiful city’), giving our friends an extra keepsake. We also managed to have our photographs taken with our friends from New Zealand and Norway, and with all the countries of the Balkans too.

We helped ourselves to a few sweets from every corner of the world, and soon afterwards it was time for dinner and for packing up the pit. Before we left, however, our students set themselves the goal of meeting one of the leading people at REV and passing on the message that the most durable part in our kit is not durable enough. Along with the letter came a necklace made of all the broken components.

The end of the event was followed by a long wait for the coaches, as our hotel is evidently rather unpopular. For us this was especially tiring, as we did not sit down on the coach until about nine o’clock in the evening, having been told that the coach to the airport would collect us at midnight. So at the hotel we quickly packed our things and set off on a last walk to the little shop that is always open. There we picked up croissants, drinks and snacks, then hurried back down the hill to the hotel, into the shower and off to the airport. On the way to the airport we also picked up one of the members of the Montenegrin team, who is currently at school in Slovenia and was therefore travelling with us.

At the airport we got the logistics done fairly quickly; more tedious was weighing all the suitcases and distributing the weight. Once we had found out at which gate we were to report, most of the team began a short sleep before it was time to board the aeroplane. We soon arrived in Belgrade, where we passed the time strolling about, watching the sunrise and playing cards. Before we knew it, we had landed in Ljubljana, and whilst waiting for our luggage we recorded a thank-you video for Zavarovalnica Triglav, the insurance company that once again helped us with our insurance this year. We Hatters waved one another goodbye and went home for a well-earned rest and a long sleep.

Until next time, pō mārie

entry.title: A Snapping Mechanism, Exploding Kittens and Clattering Soldiers’ Shoes
entry.summary: Saturday had arrived, our penultimate day in the Greek capital. The morning ritual was followed by a generous helping of work, as the robot had to be put in order before the first match of the day, which was not very long after the hour of our arrival. Unfortunately the work with the screwdrivers dragged on to such an extent that we played one match without a robot, with only our human player representing the team. So it was that we ended match number 123, in the company of Argentina and Cape Verde, against the line-up of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, the Maldives and Sudan, with a defeat (16–58).
entry.content:
Saturday had arrived, our penultimate day in the Greek capital. The morning ritual was followed by a generous helping of work, as the robot had to be put in order before the first match of the day, which was not very long after the hour of our arrival. Unfortunately the work with the screwdrivers dragged on to such an extent that we played one match without a robot, with only our human player representing the team. So it was that we ended match number 123, in the company of Argentina and Cape Verde, against the line-up of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, the Maldives and Sudan, with a defeat (16–58).

The work on the robot was not yet finished, but soon after the first official match we were scheduled to appear in the additional Skills Challenge competition, where we were supposed to show off one of the robot’s unique capabilities – something which, with a robot that did not work, we naturally did not go through with in the end. We cancelled our appearance and carried on with the servicing. After a while the robot was in a markedly more working state, with a mechanism that managed to rise. A problem arose with lifting two balls, so we were obliged to lift only one in the matches. Bending remained a problem when lifting to 120 cm, but the second match of the day came round too soon. With a whistle, match number 153 set the blue alliance, made up of Slovenia, Vietnam and the Philippines, and the red alliance, made up of Chad, Saint Lucia and Guam, off on their match. This time, once again, the red alliance carried off the win, 53–31.

We later realised that the parts critical to us (the High Strength Hex Hubs) were fitted in such a way that each one failed in turn after the one before it, until the cycle came full circle. Naturally, each breakage meant the part had to be replaced. Testing brought with it more broken components of the same kind, so the robot usually ran well for a little more than one match before it needed servicing. The complex system we designed and built is impressive, to be sure, but it has too little power, or rather too many critical points.

We carried on with the day and played in match number 209 in the company of Moldova and Turkmenistan. On the other side of the field we could see the representatives of North Macedonia, Nigeria and the Virgin Islands (the American territory). This match was of considerable importance to us, as Moldova is one of the best countries in the competition, and it was one of our rare opportunities to play alongside one of the best robots. This time the upper hand was ours, and we came back to the pit smiling and motivated after a match that ended 113–57.

Then came lunch, to which we could go somewhat less drenched in sweat, as since the morning we had been cooled by fans making up for the wrongly installed air conditioning. Soon it was time for match number 238. This time we played as a pair only, alongside Afghanistan, which sadly could not bring the rest of its team owing to problems at the border. The third member of the red alliance should have been the team from the Marshall Islands, which, however, did not appear. On the opposite side we could see the robots of the British Virgin Islands, Pakistan and Libya. Victory went to the blue alliance, 43 to 22.

The breaks between matches allowed for regular servicing and also for sampling sweets from nearly every country in the world. Sugar proved a solid raw material for points, but evidently there was not enough of it for us to finish match number 263 on the winning half. This time, on the blue side, we worked with the Federated States of Micronesia and Singapore, on whom our members pinned the nickname ‘Sigmapore’, to which they agreed, beaming from ear to ear. The red side was graced by the representatives of Costa Rica, China and Barbados. This time our side managed to earn no fewer than 85 points, but we fell 8 short. And so the match ended 93–85 to our opponents.

During the day we had the chance to look at what the American colleges WPI and MIT have to offer, and also at what Greek education, telecommunications and energy companies do. Besides this, we could also see an example of a wooden robot lady who can move with the help of legumes and pours a mixture of water and wine when a cup is placed in her palm. With these we could while away the time when we were not repairing our over-complicated mechanism.
