Serious problems proved fatal in match number 285, which was also the last of the penultimate day of competition. As before every match, we forged a strategy in advance, only this time we were conferring with Luxembourg and Antigua and Barbuda. Although our robots are meant to cooperate, this rarely shows between the blue and the red alliance, the latter made up this time of the teams from Swaziland, Lebanon and Ukraine. Sadly we ended the last match of the day with a defeat, 50–32 in figures.

After the strenuous competitive part of the day, some relaxation is only proper, and the organisers provided it at a bar next to the Peace and Friendship Stadium. There, activities awaited us such as painting watercolour tattoos, a maze, and the decimals of the number pi, after which the party was also named. Our first stop was by the entrance, where we could make a brooch of our own design. This was followed by exchanging a voucher for a soft drink of our choice. Having found a free table without seats (a standing table), we decided to start a game of Exploding Kittens on our feet. During our game, music began to play on the most open part of the dance floor, to which visitors could learn traditional Greek dances. Our few games of exploding kittens stretched out until the coaches left. Whilst waiting by the road outside the bar, we managed to pop down to the sea and dip our toes in. Our wait for the coach to the Hotel Titania was tiring, as we had to wait for the right one out of a long line of coaches, which took about an hour and a half.

On returning to the hotel, we quickly changed and went for a walk about the city. Our first visit was to the national bank, in front of which two soldiers always guard the statue of the unknown fallen soldier. On the hour, the guard changes, which is one of the sights of Athens. As we had arrived a good ten minutes before the changing began, we walked through the underpass, which, amongst other things, is also a station for the underground, but which also has an exhibition open to passers-by. We could see the remains of vessels and of walls, or rather graves. Then we popped over to a nearby park, within which a palace lies hidden, and in front of which, at the time of our visit, stood some small tents that reminded us of the DM women’s run back home.

Just in time, we joined the herd of visitors who had likewise come to watch the changing of the guard. During the changing, two less traditional, or rather less interesting, soldiers stand by a little sentry box nearby: one who will remain there for the duration of the watch, and another who will escort the two soldiers who have just completed their duty. The changing lasts a few minutes and requires visitors to stand at a suitable distance, as otherwise they are told to step back. During the changing, the two new soldiers approach, slowly raising one arm and one leg, with an audible scraping of their shoes, which have a large round pompom on the toe. The soldiers are dressed in traditional garb and wear a cap and carry a weapon at all times. After the changing, the two new soldiers each stand at their post, and the stationed (‘less traditional’) soldier comes to straighten their clothes and caps. The two traditional soldiers who have finished their watch are escorted away by one of the two less traditional soldiers, who must first clear a way through the crowd so that they can pass.

After that we decided to look at a park that resembled Park Zvezda back home, with a fountain in the middle. Some members of the team stopped with a mentor for dinner at KFC, whilst the others went back to the hotel to rest, looking for cross-body bags on the way.

Until next time, تصبح على خير

entry.content:
After a long night and a short sleep, we opened our eyes to the first day of competition. The same morning ritual and the journey to the Peace and Friendship Stadium were followed by the promised session of repairs to the robot, or more precisely to the ball-catching mechanism. After a short test session we changed our approach, opting for one similar to the solution of our colleagues from Norway. We built the ‘cage’ from aluminium profiles and shafts fitted with collars, which reduced friction and so let the ball glide along, turning freely on the shafts.

As time passes ever more quickly the closer one comes to the ranked matches, we did not manage to fit the new mechanism, which would have needed additional programming of its components in order to work properly. For that reason, we dashed off to our first serious match, number 22, which we played alongside Morocco and Tunisia. Unfortunately we were beaten 24–32 by the blue alliance, made up of Iraq, Italy and Laos.

Minor repairs and the opening practice gave us extra motivation, which came to the fore in our second match, number 51, which we played in the company of the teams from Montenegro and the Cayman Islands. This time we finished with a stronger score of no fewer than 55 points, which the opposing alliance nevertheless managed to equal. In the match against Niger, Belarus and the Cook Islands, there was no winner.

Soon it was time for lunch, which, together with the match we had all but won, gave us extra energy. Once again the whistle announced the start of a match, this time number 82. We joined forces with Cyprus and Ecuador and won 48–42 against Angola, Algeria and Botswana.

The last match before our scheduled multicultural dinner was number 102. This time, on the red side, we worked with Japan and Uruguay. All was running smoothly until something in the robot made an unpleasant noise, followed by a very crooked trajectory of the lifting mechanism. On top of this mishap, we had to replay the match from the start because the field elements malfunctioned (when the condition was met – a blue and a green ball in the basket – the orange ball was not released). One last attempt to use the lifting mechanism resulted in a change of strategy, to the extent that we merely ferried hand-loaded balls to the collection area on the floor. Alas, this time we countries of the red alliance ended up in the red on the scoreboard too, as the match finished 57–77. With that, we ended the first day of ranked matches with 1 win, 1 draw and 2 defeats.

The time had come to change into somewhat different clothes. This time we chose T-shirts bearing the word ‘Slovenija’ and, when called, set off by coach for the Stavros Niarchos cultural centre. On the coach to the Athenian answer to Ljubljana’s Špica or Tivoli, we were kept company by members of the Slovak team from the hilly north of their country. A stroll past the building and the still water of the cultural centre gave nothing away as yet, but round the corner the glass part of the building revealed itself, its interior, floor by floor, reminiscent of the renovated Cukrarna, Ljubljana’s old sugar refinery. The place is evidently much frequented by people out walking, who linger in the café or gather on the nearby lawn. We followed the volunteers carrying ‘FIRST Global Challenge’ signs, and so our way led up a ramp, then through a small park with low trees and a lawn, and up yet another ramp to the top of the cultural centre. There, all 193 teams were greeted by music, a panoramic view and a variety of food (the ice-cream bar opened later).

And so we ended the day with music and food and a view of the sunset. Unfortunately our departure was delayed, although the day was meant to close with the drummers’ performance and dance. So we left for home some two hours late; some of us went off to a well-earned rest, whilst others brandished playing cards before bed.

Until next time, god natt

entry.title: Let’s Meet at the Olympic Rings
entry.summary: The robotics olympiad has begun! 26 September had arrived, the first of four days for our Olympic robotics team. Another hearty breakfast and the journey to the Peace and Friendship Stadium were followed by settling into our pit once more and handing in our robot’s technical documentation.
entry.content:
The robotics olympiad has begun! 26 September had arrived, the first of four days for our Olympic robotics team. Another hearty breakfast and the journey to the Peace and Friendship Stadium were followed by settling into our pit once more and handing in our robot’s technical documentation.

Aware that a long day lay ahead of us, we decided to save our energy and practise driving the robot. Our booking of a practice field came round soon after we arrived, and so the two drivers and the two human players could practise. At the end of an intensive driving session, after some fifteen minutes, we discovered that the robot was noticeably weaker owing to a broken component – otherwise reckoned one of the sturdiest – on the lifting mechanism of our box. Replacing it was relatively simple, as the two High Strength Hubs were located directly behind the drive motor and on the assembly with the driven shaft.

During practice we realised that more points could be gained if we could bring the orange ball, which represents food obtained from water and energy, to the human player. The original idea involved pushing the ball along, which, however, is rather unpredictable. We therefore decided to build a fence for the ball, with which we could reliably push, or rather drag, the ball to the human players. The first prototypes consisted of structural elements of clear plastic (polycarbonate), cardboard and sticky tape, the whole thing driven by two servo motors. The additional component was a challenge of its own, as it had to be able to tow the rubber ball steadily and also fold away compactly enough for the robot not to exceed the size limit of 50x50x50 cm. The first attempts proved qualified successes, as the robot could tow the ball behind it, but only very slowly. Turning the robot in a circle also posed a great problem, as, just as when towing too fast, the ball could escape owing to the plastic component bending.

The working part of our day soon came to an end, with lunch in between and a very early dinner, followed by time to change into the traditional dress in which the teams were to represent their countries at the opening ceremony. For the last three years, our team’s non-national costume has been the shirt of our secondary school – Vegova Ljubljana – so changing shirts was no great drain on our time. With that, we finished work for Thursday and left the rest of the fitting of the robot’s new mechanism for the following day. Before leaving for the opening ceremony, we tidied our workspace and played a round of the card game Uno Flip, which caught the attention of some passers-by; they could not join in, however, as we were called to begin our way to the coach just as the game ended.

We set off in a line together with our neighbours from Slovakia and the Solomon Islands. On the way to the Olympic stadium (the Panathenaic Stadium), we were treated to karaoke led by members of the Slovak team. When we arrived in front of the stadium, a long queue of our fellow competitors and other visitors to the free event awaited us.

We two mentors were soon separated from the students and joined the herd hurrying to the tiered seats as close as possible to the stage, where a DJ was playing music as we arrived. Before long the two hosts greeted us, and we could watch pre-prepared videos about the purpose of the FIRST Global Challenge olympiad. This was followed by an opening performance from a dance group, and after that by the parade of flags, in which 193 teams (each from its own country) could step onto the stage in national costume and wave their flags.

The festive sea of flags was followed by a speech from the founder of FIRST, Mr Dean Kamen. After a lengthy speech on the importance of the programme in which we take part, as it brings unity and the knowledge needed to achieve a better tomorrow, there followed a performance by the Black Eyed Peas.

The good tunes ended all too soon, and with them the opening ceremony. We made our way to the coach back to the hotel, where well-earned sleep awaited one of us, and a walk to the nearby McDonald’s the rest.

Until next time, gudnaet

entry.title: Friends Old and New
entry.summary: We began our Wednesday with a hearty breakfast at sunrise on the roof of the Hotel Titania, which we had to reach by way of the emergency stairs, as the lifts were all taken. On the 11th floor a crush of people awaited us, along with a view of the Acropolis. The shortage of cutlery was made up for by the tasty food, which we had to clear from our plates quickly so as not to miss the coach, as had happened to some countries, whilst some others had not even arrived in Athens yet.
entry.content:
We began our Wednesday with a hearty breakfast at sunrise on the roof of the Hotel Titania, which we had to reach by way of the emergency stairs, as the lifts were all taken. On the 11th floor a crush of people awaited us, along with a view of the Acropolis. The shortage of cutlery was made up for by the tasty food, which we had to clear from our plates quickly so as not to miss the coach, as had happened to some countries, whilst some others had not even arrived in Athens yet.

The coaches full of Olympians took the motorway to the Peace and Friendship Stadium. The Olympic arena stands right by the sea and has a curved roof in the shape of a crisp. With every coach, the rising temperatures were joined by the voices of team members waiting impatiently for the entrance doors to open. In the meantime we had the chance to greet old friends, namely the teams of Slovakia and Norway. The chatter and the befriending of new members passed quickly, and it was time for each country to find its place in the Olympic alphabet, unpack its tools and begin work on its robot.

Our settling in to the corner bearing the sign ‘Slovenija’ was enlivened by old friends from South Africa, Slovakia and the Solomon Islands. After that we unpacked the robot and began a small post-transport service, which was interrupted by a great misfortune – the chain slipped off one of the sprockets of our lifting mechanism, owing to the unfortunate position of a nut and bolt, and then jammed between the sprocket and the aluminium profile. On top of that, the chain had not been assembled correctly. We soon took the chain apart, mended it, threaded it back on and joined both ends together. The robot’s chassis was ready; all that remained was to test the lifting mechanism, which resembles a pair of scissors.

With the help of elastic bands, the lifting mechanism was capable of raising two balls. Concern arose amongst the team members over the whole mechanism tilting as it rose or descended. Since its path was the same going up as coming down, we decided to leave the mechanism as it was. There followed a few test lifts and some adjustment of the ramp that lets the balls roll of their own accord towards the exit of the box. In doing so, we had to adjust the incline, as an under-inflated ball could escape from the box if the robot stopped suddenly.

During the repairs, our mentor Luka brought a box of team shirts, bags, bottles and other small gifts that every country receives. We could at last exchange our sweaty clothes for sports shirts, and soon afterwards we discovered that the cause of the heat in every country’s workspace was a wrongly installed air-conditioning unit, with its outdoor unit at our end. After that we decided to start a worldwide flag exchange, in which every country can have a Slovenian flag if it leaves its own with us.

Soon after these moments of gift-giving, we went to lunch, which involved quite a few menus and a large hall that is otherwise a gymnasium with basketball courts. After lunch with our friends from Norway, we went back to our pit full of energy, where, soon after our return, we had the opportunity to get the robot inspection done. The lady examined our robot thoroughly and, after a demonstration of its workings, said that we had done a wonderful job. She forgot to give us the sticker for passing inspection and the LED-light indicator that shows which side (alliance) one is playing for, so we received those later.

After the inspection the students split up, some marching off to the practice fields and the others going to get to know the other teams, or rather countries. In the meantime the two mentors minded our pit and chatted with the mentors of other teams.

Once all the students had gathered at the workspace again, we heard over the loudspeakers about the drivers’ meeting, which we had also spotted on the schedule published in advance. Over the course of the meeting, a good hour long, the drivers and the so-called human players learnt more about the rules for running the matches themselves. Straight after the meeting ended, an opportunity for a practice match arose, and one call later the robot was already on its way.

After quite some time the students returned, just in time for dinner, as luck would have it. This time, too, we went in two shifts on a walk of a few minutes around the entire arena to reach the dining hall, where a new menu and another hearty meal awaited us. After dinner we tidied up our pit and went to catch the coach home. Before turning in, we made our final corrections to our documentation and arranged with the staff at the hotel reception for it to be printed.

Until next time, dobru noc
